lens: FIT TO THE USER: how much real logic is in Rust and whether it is idiomatic, simple and non-slop; genuinely concurrent and async (bounded parallelism, cancellation, no UI blocking); end-user experience (one right-click, clear progress, one login prompt, sensible failure messages).

scores.justification: Best literal fit to the two hard requirements. The per-item pipeline is real async Rust (async fn, select_biased!, FuturesUnordered) on a small sans-IO executor in zero-import wasm. Per-item and per-host gates, token buckets, the licence ledger, hedging, timeouts on virtual time and tier escalation are all decided in Rust. JS is about 1.7k lines of effect runner (est. ~82% Rust by lines vs ~72% for failure-first). Cancellation is the most idiomatic of the three: dropping a future emits cancel and release effects in the same StepOut, with generation-checked task keys. The discover_oa sample reads as ordinary async Rust, and the sim tests with virtual time prove the licence limits natively. This also answers failure-first's claim that Rust cannot await I/O from zero-import wasm; research SUMMARY (b) and 03 §3 make the zero-import hand ABI the proven path, and this design shows futures can sit on top of it. UX is good: one LoginGate sign-in per epoch and no re-prompt loops, per-row status with Fluent args, hand-off buttons, an end-of-run report with ledger usage. It is held back by (a) the items permit staying held while an item is parked on the LoginGate, (b) HTML parsing staying on the main thread, (c) thinner failure coverage than failure-first, and (d) some defensive machinery (try_borrow_mut everywhere, thread_local globals, LOST_WAKE sweep, deferred-cancel queue) that edges toward over-engineering.
fatal_flaws: Serious but trivially fixable: run_item acquires the 4-slot items permit and keeps it through institutional and LoginGate waits (design §3.3 vs §2.4). Once four items are parked on a sign-in prompt, the remaining 16 items, including ones OA could fetch, stall for up to the 300 s login timeout. This contradicts the claim that OA work for other items continues. Fix: drop the permit (RAII) before awaiting the LoginGate and re-acquire with priority, as the other two designs do.

The 'about 45 ms for 2 MiB' main-thread parse figure is the hand-scanner extrapolation. research/07-rust-wasm-toolchain.md:196 gives html5gum ~320 ms for 6 MB, so ~107 ms for 2 MiB, repeated for up to 4 concurrent items on Zotero's UI thread. 'Never block the UI' is only partly met until the pure instance moves to the ChromeWorker that research/03 §3 proved works. The pure instance is stateless and its effect handlers are already async, so the move is cheap, but the design defers it to v2.

The engine trap path restarts unfinished items once from a coarse JS journal. That can re-issue publisher requests on the institutional route and loses all in-flight state, where failure-first isolates the fault to one item. The risk is low because the engine never sees raw HTML, but the recovery is the weakest of the three.

The hand-rolled executor, reactor and waker are the largest bug surface. A lost wakeup is a silent stall, and wasm gives no Rust stack. The mitigations (stall watchdog, dump_state, sim tests) are good but must be built.

Lacks a login-ineffective state (cookies not reused), a bounded prompt count per run and an offline state. Items that bounce on the IdP after a sign-in each burn a second hidden-browser load, and there is no network-down handling.
PDF bodies are held as ArrayBuffers in a 192 MiB BodyStore. The Rust-side bytes semaphore bounds this, but it is less lean than the file-sink streaming in failure-first.

scores.justification: Cleanest and most testable Rust (pure decision functions plus one small sans-IO scheduler with submit/poll/complete/cancel and a next_wake_ms), and the policy side is genuinely strong. The sequencing, concurrency, cancellation and timeouts are JS, though, which is precisely what the user stressed: 'concurrent and async' and 'Rust wherever possible'. The design says so itself: ~60% Rust by lines, with the item FSM, hedging, parking, CancelScope tree, Semaphore, TaskSet and firstSuccess in JS and tested only against Node fakes. Its justification, that making Rust drive effects only adds a message protocol without moving logic, is undercut by rust-async-engine, which shows the orchestration itself can live in zero-import wasm. The 'JS never inspects URLs or bodies' rule is enforced by an ast-grep regex, which indirection defeats. Correctness of unhandled rejections, leaked timers and promise lifetimes depends on discipline, not the compiler. UX is the second best of the three: a Tools-menu 'Sign In to King's…' warm-up, a Full Text Options submenu, parked items that release slots with priority re-acquire, immediate Deferred{cap} outcomes, a progress window that survives being closed, and hand-offs. Parsing still runs on the main thread (est. ~110 ms worst case), and the scheduler cannot see hidden-browser hops or translator requests.
fatal_flaws: Orchestration, concurrency, cancellation and timeout policy are JS. Rust is ~60% of lines and decides branches, but does not run the pipeline. This is the weakest fit to 'Rust wherever possible' and to the user's concurrent/async requirement.

Correct concurrency rests on discipline plus Node fakes (FakeHttp, FakeBrowser), not on the compiler or on native deterministic simulation of the item pipeline. Only the scheduler is sim-tested in cargo. The self-listed risk of Node fakes diverging from real Zotero is accurate.
The JS-never-inspects-strings boundary is convention plus a regex lint, so policy and sequencing can drift between the two languages.
Parsing and S/D wasm calls run on the main thread with only an idle() hop; a 2 MiB page is ~110 ms of UI stall by its own estimate, and there is no worker plan beyond 'async-shaped facade'.
Each HTTP request costs three JSON round trips into the scheduler (submit, poll, complete). That is acceptable at this scale but adds protocol surface without moving the pipeline into Rust.

scores.justification: Highest quality on the end-user side and on keeping the UI unblocked. Roughly 70-75% Rust, with a deterministic sans-IO engine and about 95% of decisions in Rust. It has a 32-row failure catalogue where every row has a signal, response and test ID. It has a per-realm session machine with Expired, Declined, TimedOut, Refused (Conditional Access), Ineffective, Misconfigured and Suspended states, and prompt caps. A single-flight interactive gate, parked items that release slots and OA work that never waits on login. All untrusted bytes go through a ChromeWorker analyser with a 3 s watchdog and respawn, which is the only design that actually keeps parsing off the UI thread (research/03 §3 and the probe show ChromeWorker and fetch of chrome:// work). PDFs stream to disk through Zotero.HTTP.download (credentials 'include', http.js:719), and the design correctly notes abort surfaces as TimeoutException (http.js:737-738). It also has a grouped end-of-run report ('Needs you / Not found / Failed / Skipped / Attached') and a 'Retry with sign-in' action. Against it: the Rust is hand-written event/effect state machines, not async Rust, and the stated reason is wrong. A Rust future can await an op completed by event, as rust-async-engine does. The item FSM, which merges parallel lookups, hedging, tiers and sessions into explicit enum states, will be the biggest and hardest-to-read file. Checkpoint, journal and replay need strict determinism and high-water dedupe to protect a rare event, which is gold-plating given the engine never parses hostile input. There are three wasm contexts and a large effect protocol.
fatal_flaws: Not async Rust. The 'cannot await I/O' rationale for event/state-machine style is incorrect, and the explicit FSM for a concurrent pipeline is more code, more error-prone and less readable than async fn with join and select. That weakens 'simple, idiomatic, non-slop' against the user's Rust request.

Checkpoint/journal/replay trap recovery relies on perfect determinism (BTreeMap only, seeded PRNG, no hidden clock). A single leak silently corrupts recovery, and the design admits this. It is the most complex mechanism in any of the designs and guards a low-probability event.
ProgressQueue has no per-item cancel or row actions, so users get two surfaces (queue dialog plus report window) and Cancel only cancels everything.

Timeouts are chosen by the engine but enforced by per-effect JS timers (first byte, idle, total), so timing policy is split across the boundary, unlike virtual-time timeouts in Rust in rust-async-engine.
Unverified assumptions it flags itself: HTTP.download honouring a custom User-Agent, and posting a WebAssembly.Module to a ChromeWorker (the fallback of fetching chrome:// in the worker is viable).
Heaviest build: ~8-9k Rust plus ~3.3k JS, three wasm contexts, and a long advanced-prefs list. Highest chance of schedule slip for a single-user plugin.

best_ideas_to_graft: From failure-first: the failure catalogue F1-F32 as the acceptance-test list for the async engine; each row becomes a Rust Outcome variant or a sim-test scenario.

From failure-first: the per-realm session state machine (Expired, Declined, TimedOut, Refused with Conditional Access code, Ineffective, Misconfigured, Suspended), with at most 2 prompts per realm per run, 'Keep waiting', and a 'Retry with sign-in' action. This fills rust-async-engine's missing 'login not reused' and re-prompt-cap states.

From failure-first: parked items must release their active slot and resume with priority. Put it in rust-async-engine as dropping the items permit before awaiting LoginGate, and re-acquire with priority. This fixes the batch-stall flaw.

From failure-first: host the stateless parser/analyser instance in a ChromeWorker with a 3 s watchdog, terminate and respawn, and requeue-once. Do it in v1, not v2, because the pure instance is already stateless and its effect handlers are already async. Research 03 §3 shows ChromeWorker and wasm work.

From failure-first: stream institutional and large PDFs to disk with Zotero.HTTP.download (sink file, cookies included at http.js:719) and track the true abort cause in JS. Also add state.json for the ledger and temp-dir sweep, a NetworkDown pause, a soft XMP DOI identity check, and strict Crossref title matching for items without a DOI.
From failure-first: the grouped end-of-run report ('Needs you / Not found / Failed / Skipped / Attached') with copy-diagnostics that redacts URLs and strips cookies.

From js-orchestrator-pure-rust: a Tools-menu 'Sign In to King's…' warm-up so users can sign in once before a batch, a 'Full Text Options' submenu to keep the context menu to one visible entry, and immediate Deferred{cap} outcomes when licence limits bite, so a capped item never holds a slot.

From js-orchestrator-pure-rust: inst.plan as a pure Rust function returning ordered steps, skipped steps with reasons and hand-off URLs, so 'direct' is not re-tried on a host that already showed no_access in this run. Also keep the ast-grep boundary lint on the JS runner to stop policy creeping back into JS.
From js-orchestrator-pure-rust: closing the progress window does not cancel the run, with a small ProgressWindow headline to reopen it.

From rust-async-engine (keep as the core): drop-is-cancel futures with cancel and release effects emitted in the same StepOut, virtual-time timeouts, a poll budget with 'more', reserve-then-commit licence ledger, trace/dump_state and the stall watchdog, a ref-counted MIME dispatcher keyed by channel topFrameElement, and the discover_oa shape (FuturesUnordered with an early-settle select).

Cross-cutting fix for the base: correct the main-thread parse estimate to the html5gum figure (~107 ms for 2 MiB, from research/07:196) and replace the defensive try_borrow_mut/LOST_WAKE/deferred-cancel layers with a design where re-entrant borrows cannot happen. Run the sim tests with a seeded schedule so a bug panics loudly instead of being swallowed.
recommended_base: rust-async-engine: the Rust async engine (sans-IO executor in zero-import wasm with a thin JS effect runner) is the base. It matches the user's two explicit requirements most literally, has the smallest total code (~9k lines vs ~12k for failure-first), and is easiest to graft onto. Failure-first's gaps are filled by adding failure-first's session states, release-on-park behaviour, ChromeWorker analyser, file-sink downloads and grouped report to this engine; adding the async pipeline to failure-first would need a rewrite.

lens: Buildability and testability: can parallel implementation agents build this correctly in one pass from clear contracts (boundary complexity, debuggability inside Zotero, size of the riskiest component, native/Node testability, integration risk, size of the JS surface that only Zotero can test)

scores.justification: Strong native testability, but it has the most delicate single component. WHY IT TESTS WELL: the engine is sans-IO, so the exact shipped code (exec.rs, reactor.rs, sched/, pipeline/) runs natively under a SimHost with a virtual clock. The invariant list in section 6.2 is the best concurrency test spec of the three (every op completed or cancelled once, no BodyHandle leak, no stall, seeded random completion orders, golden effect traces). A single export, fx_step, plus the pure fx_call keeps the Rust/JS surface narrow. Async/await is also the most natural way to write the per-item pipeline (compare failure-first's hand-rolled FSMs). Native replay of a recorded StepIn log would reproduce any in-Zotero bug with a real backtrace. Total JS is only about 1,700 lines. WHY IT LOSES POINTS: (1) The riskiest component is a hand-built executor with drop-based cancellation, generation-checked slab keys, a thread_local ready queue and LOST_WAKE, then an async pipeline of about 2,750 lines on futures-util (FuturesUnordered, select_biased!, hedging, LoginGate wakers). Nothing like it exists in spikes/wasm-spike. The spike proved only synchronous JSON calls (js/fulltext-core.js:58-99). (2) Serial critical path: exec, reactor, proto and the typed Op wrappers must be right before any pipeline lane can be exercised, so parallel agents are blocked early. (3) Its Rc<RefCell<Sched>> shared by item futures is exactly the lint-invisible panic class that research/07-rust-wasm-toolchain.md:323 warns about. Under panic=abort a BorrowMutError traps the whole engine and loses every in-flight run. The design mitigates with try_borrow_mut helpers and deferred cancel, but any agent writing pipeline code can violate it. It never mentions clippy::await_holding_refcell_ref. (4) Debuggability inside Zotero is the worst of the three: async state is opaque in stripped wasm, a trap gives only the panic-hook string, and recovery is lossy (restart-once re-issues requests). (5) The ABI adds fx_stage ownership transfer ('JS must NOT free a staged buffer', blob ids, auto-free at end of next call) on top of the proven borrow-in/free-after ABI. The spike already has a simpler two-buffer raw call (fulltext-core.js:74-88). (6) It is unmeasured: futures-util with the zero-import guarantee, size, and two 420 KB instances are 'only gated in xtask'. Cu.now() is used for monotonic time but appears in no probe (grep of research/ finds nothing). (7) About 1.3k JS lines (net, browser, login, adapter, ui, bootstrap) can still only be tested in a real Zotero.
fatal_flaws: Custom executor and reactor are the critical path, are not covered by any spike, and a RefCell or logic panic traps the engine and loses all in-flight state (07:323).
Engine trap recovery is restart-once from a JS journal, so it can re-issue publisher requests. The reserve-then-commit ledger softens this for licence limits only.
fx_stage ownership-transfer ABI is new, stateful and easy to leak or double-free across a trap between stage and call. A plain two-buffer call (as in the spike) avoids it.
futures-util zero-import and size claim is unverified. Fallback is about 150 lines of hand-written join/select, which is more custom async code to test.
Debugging a field failure inside Zotero relies on trace effects and dump_state. There is no JS stack through the orchestration.

scores.justification: Highest probability of a correct one-pass build by parallel agents, at the cost of a lower Rust share. WHY: (1) It has the smallest boundary and the only one already proven. The ABI is the spike's ABI (alloc/free, JSON in with packed u64 out, raw two-buffer HTML call, fx_sniff_pdf) plus a few ops. Every call is synchronous request/response with no callbacks, wakers or re-entrancy. js/fulltext-core.js:58-107 already implements call(), landingRaw(), sniffPdf() and reset(), and 03-zotero-runtime-probe.md:104-110 proves the pattern in all five JS contexts. (2) Contracts decompose cleanly into independent lanes. The Rust side is the op catalogue (ids, oa.requests/parse, cand.rank, fx_page, url.classify, inst.*, proxy.*, attach.clean_url), each a pure function checked against fixtures/html/expected.json and fixtures/oa/manifest.json. The scheduler has a tiny protocol (submit/poll/complete/cancel/snapshot) and is sim-tested natively with a seeded PRNG. The JS ports (Http, Browser, Translators, Save) sit behind fakes. Only the op-schema freeze is on the critical path. (3) It has the best debuggability: JS stack traces, Browser Toolbox, one logged op per Rust call, a stateless decider D that resets in under 1 ms, and a stateful scheduler S that fails closed. (4) The riskiest component is conventional async/await JS (CancelScope tree, Semaphore, TaskSet, firstSuccess/hedge, pump, item FSM, LoginCoordinator), with the policy checks held in Rust. (5) It has the most concrete E2E plan. There is a Zotero.ZoteroFullText test hook, an --e2e dist that loads content/test/e2e.js only when the harness pref is set, scenarios E1-E10, a stale-wasm check (meta.build equals the manifest version), and a dev-proxy that refuses real profiles. Total JS is about 3.3k lines, of which about 1.2k (ports, windows, menus, bootstrap) is Zotero-only. About 2k of orchestration is Node-testable with fake ports. WHY NOT 9-10: sequencing and escalation are tested only under Node fakes, and promise and timer ordering with a FakeClock is flakier than Rust sim. The 'JS never inspects URLs or bodies' rule is convention plus an ast-grep lint, and §3.3's fetch sub-machine already encodes route-specific policy in JS (OA skip versus institutional complete(challenge), hop limits, retry-once, depth 1 versus 2). Many JSON op schemas have no shared typed definition across serde and JS. Rust share is about 60%, which is lower than the others.
fatal_flaws: Policy and sequencing drift: fetch.js and item-task.js hold real tier-escalation policy (§3.3), but only Node fakes test them, and the boundary rule is a heuristic ast-grep lint that indirection can evade.

Fidelity of Node fakes for Zotero.HTTP, HiddenBrowser and PageData is unproven. Only the harness closes this gap, and it takes about 18 s per run (zotero-harness/README.md:108-111), so E2E scenarios must be batched.
E8 (ledger persistence across restarts) depends on a harness -KeepProfile flag that does not exist. grep of tools/zotero-harness/run.ps1 finds no match.
Licence ledger lives in a user-editable pref (inst.ledger). That is acceptable as a self-limiter, but the 'persisted ledger' tests prove less than state.json plus reserve-before-fetch would.
Browser sessions count as one fetch for licence accounting, so redirector, IdP and SAML hops are not individually scheduled.

scores.justification: The best-specified test plan, but the biggest scope and the most moving parts for a one-pass build. STRENGTHS: the failure catalogue F1-F32 maps each failure to a signal, a response, an owner and a test ID (S01-S23, H01-H08). That is a ready acceptance matrix and the strongest test-driven spec of the three. The sans-IO engine makes every failure path a native state transition under a virtual clock. The serialisable engine state plus event journal means any field bug can be exported and replayed natively with a backtrace. Property tests cover replay determinism and licence caps. WHY IT SCORES LOWER ON BUILDABILITY: (1) It is the largest build, at about 8-9k Rust and 3.3k JS. The engine is hand-written per-item FSMs, a session FSM, an interactive gate, a scheduler and budgets in one Engine::step. Every type must be serde-checkpointable and deterministic (BTreeMap only, seeded PRNG, no clock reads). That is a heavy constraint that parallel agents will break silently. (2) The recovery machinery (fx_engine_export every 64 events, journal, replay minus the poisoning event, fx high-water dedupe, EngineFault injection, 3-trap abort) is a whole subsystem whose only trigger is a trap. It is invisible in normal operation and hard to test inside Zotero. The replay interplay with still-live JS timers and in-flight fetches is intricate. (3) The ChromeWorker analyser adds an async cross-thread boundary (transfer, 3 s watchdog, terminate/respawn, requeue-once) for a benefit research rates as optional. A typical page costs 1-5 ms (SUMMARY.md:87, 07 §2.2). Module postMessage is unverified. The worker has no Zotero or Services (03-zotero-runtime-probe.md:227), so its logs and failures are harder to see. (4) It has the largest Zotero-only JS surface, about 2k of 3.3k lines: file sinks via HTTP.download (UA header behaviour unverified by its own admission), tmp-dir ledger and sweep, state.json store, fx dedupe, generation guards, hard caps, ProgressQueue integration and a separate report window. (5) The event/effect protocol is wide (about 14 events, 14 effects, ref:file handles, CheckPdf/Save round trips) and the JS executor can only be checked against Node mocks. Tick against the async-engine: explicit FSMs are more code and more bug surface than the same logic written as async fn.
fatal_flaws: Checkpoint/journal/replay depends on total engine determinism. One hidden nondeterminism (HashMap iteration, float, clock read) silently corrupts recovery, and a deterministic poison event can retrap on replay.

Single monolithic Engine::step couples item FSM, session FSM, gate, scheduler and budget in a fixed service order, so parallel agents cannot build lanes independently. Integration risk is concentrated in one crate.
ChromeWorker analyser and watchdog add a failure mode and an async boundary that v1 does not need. A watchdog restart drops and requeues unrelated in-flight analyses.
HTTP.download with sink:'file', custom User-Agent and abortReason mapping rests on unverified Zotero behaviour (design's own weakness list). Any mismatch breaks the main PDF path.
Largest Zotero-only JS surface, and its correctness is exercised mainly through Node mocks plus 18 s harness runs.

best_ideas_to_graft: [from rust-async-engine] Deterministic simulation harness, applied to the Rust Scheduler S and mirrored in Node. SimHost is a virtual clock plus scripted fixture responses that record every effect. Invariants are asserted after every step: <=1 in flight per host, <=2 institutional, PDF spacing >=5 s, ledger caps incl. across export/import restart, every ticket completed or cancelled exactly once, no stall. Add seeded random-interleaving property tests and golden traces in tests/golden. Drive the Node orchestrator tests with the same scripted scenarios.

[from rust-async-engine] Reserve-then-commit licence ledger: reserve a slot and persist before emitting an institutional PDF fetch, commit on a verified PDF, roll back on non-PDF or cancel. Safer than commit-after-fetch, and it survives an S trap.

[from rust-async-engine] LoginGate epoch semantics for the JS LoginCoordinator: an epoch counter bumps on each successful sign-in. An item that failed under an older epoch retries silently once instead of re-prompting. Add Declined{run} so a declined run never reopens a window.

[from rust-async-engine] xtask gates, run in CI: empty wasm import section, export set equals ABI manifest, no C:\Users strings, size budget, plus Node ABI tests with a debug-panic build (poison, reset, replay config). Add a JS stall watchdog (tickets pending, nothing in flight, no next_wake_ms) fed by sched.snapshot.

[from failure-first] Adopt the failure catalogue F1-F32 verbatim as the acceptance matrix, and its scenario IDs S01-S23 (cargo sim) and H01-H08 (harness), assigned across Rust core, Node orchestrator and harness lanes.

[from failure-first] Runtime state in <profile>/zotero-fulltext/state.json via IOUtils.writeJSON with tmpPath, debounced, instead of the inst.ledger pref. It holds the ledger, suspended_until, EZproxy host cache, Alma cache, tmp_dirs and windows_sso_set_by_us. Also record tmp dirs before use and sweep them on startup, add the generation counter, and record an explicit abortReason because HTTP.download reports every abort as a TimeoutException.

[from failure-first] Field-repro journal, applied to S only: in debug mode log every sched.* call as (op, args, now) so a cargo test can replay it natively with a backtrace. Do not adopt full engine checkpoint/replay.
[from failure-first] NetworkDown handling (pause new fetches, probe every 15 s for 2 min, then fail with offline) and hard-cap tripwires in the JS executor, logged as invariant violations.

[from the shared spike] Keep the spike ABI as the contract: borrow-in/free-after, packed u64 output, raw two-buffer fx_page/fx_pdf_inspect (js/fulltext-core.js:58-107). Reject fx_stage ownership transfer. Replace Cu.now() with Date.now() or a probed ChromeUtils.now() (nothing in research/ probes Cu.now).

[from the base design] Zotero.ZoteroFullText test hook, --e2e dist that includes content/test/e2e.js only when the harness result-file pref is set, meta.build equals manifest version stale-wasm refusal, the dev-proxy that refuses real profiles, and the ast-grep boundary lint. Strengthen the lint by also failing CI if fetch.js or item-task.js import any URL parsing helper.

[tooling] If any async Rust is added later (e.g. moving the item FSM into Rust), deny clippy::await_holding_refcell_ref and clippy::await_holding_lock workspace-wide from day one, and forbid RefCell in shared scheduler state.
recommended_base: js-orchestrator-pure-rust. It is the only design whose boundary is already proven by the spike (synchronous JSON ops, raw two-buffer calls, poison and reset). It also splits into independent lanes: pure Rust ops against the existing fixtures, a sans-IO scheduler with native sim tests, JS ports behind fakes, and UI/xtask/harness. Add three things from the others: the failure-first catalogue as the acceptance matrix, state.json plus the reserve-then-commit ledger, and the async-engine's sim invariants and LoginGate epochs. If the user's 'Rust wherever possible' requirement is later enforced strictly, rust-async-engine is the better second choice than failure-first, because it is smaller and its pipeline is async fn rather than hand-written FSMs. It should be built only after the pure core and scheduler lanes (shared with the base) have landed, and only with the RefCell and clippy guards above.

lens: WILL IT ACTUALLY WORK: correctness against Zotero 10.0.6 / Gecko 140 realities and the research evidence. I checked API claims in .ref/omni-app and the briefs (SUMMARY, 03, 08). I also built a throwaway zero-import wasm probe of design A's executor core (Arc<Wake> + thread_local ready queue + FuturesUnordered + select_biased! + Drop-cancel + virtual timers). It compiled to 36 KB with an empty import section and behaved correctly under Node: out-of-order completion, timeout, and cancel effects on drop. So A's central mechanism is feasible, and the risk in all three designs is in the Gecko/Zotero effect layer, not the Rust engine.

scores.justification: Most evidence-consistent on the mechanics it names: zero-import ABI, per-channel PDF capture (onContent receives the channel: mimeTypeHandler.js:287-292), refcounted MIME registration, reserve-then-commit ledger, bytes semaphore, stall watchdog, plain UA via a User-Agent header (VersionHeader leaves a UA without 'Zotero/' alone: zotero.js:2313-2316, matching 08 §6.2), and the createURLAttachmentFromTemporaryStorageDirectory save path (attachments.js:682-736). My probe shows the executor design works. It scores lowest because it has the most unproven surface for the least gain. Every Gecko interaction (login polling, settle, capture) is split between Rust decisions and JS loops over a large JSON protocol that only a live Zotero can fully exercise, and a lost wake or a mismatched ignored-completion/BodyStore handle shows up as a silent stall with no Rust stack trace. It also hard-codes timeouts that contradict measured behaviour.
fatal_flaws: Landing-page timeout is 20 s (22 s JS backstop), and institutional attempts get no hedge and no retry. 08 §3.6 measured Wiley abstract/landing responses at 25-37 s and over 60 s twice. The Wiley institutional route, a core medical publisher, would time out on most items. There is no slow-host profile (design C has one).

HiddenBrowser.load() is not handled. It rejects after 5 s with no top-level location change and returns false (HiddenBrowser.mjs:183-187, 231-239), and it always does so for PDF responses because the MIME handler aborts the original listener (mimeTypeHandler.js:185-187). The browser_load effect says only 'load, settle'. It must ignore load()'s result and use its own progress listener as BrowserRequest._loadAndSettle does (browserRequest.js:464-483, load() deliberately not awaited at :483). Otherwise slow publishers and PDF captures are reported as failures.
All untrusted HTML parsing (html5gum, up to 2 MiB) plus DOMParser/translators run on the main thread. The ChromeWorker offload is deferred to v2, so a 4-item batch can jank the UI repeatedly.

A trap in the engine instance loses all in-flight state. Journal recovery restarts unfinished items once, which can re-issue institutional publisher requests. Only the reserve-before-fetch ledger bounds this, so the risk falls on the licence-sensitive path.

UI claim is wrong: ProgressWindow.addDescription only builds text and label nodes with attributes (progressWindow.js:208-235), so a 'Details...' link that opens the report window cannot be done this way. Minor, but it contradicts the source.

Per-host institutional gating is keyed on the request host, but the first hop is doi.org or go.openathens.net and the real publisher host is only known after redirects. A 1-per-host limit cannot be enforced for those hops without a no-follow probe (shared with B and C, but A states the HostKey gate as if it were exact).

scores.justification: The most conventional design and the least likely to hit protocol-level integration bugs. Zotero/Gecko objects (HTTP, HiddenBrowser, PageData, login window, MIME capture) are driven directly from JS, and Rust is called only through synchronous JSON ops, so every effect can be debugged with JS stacks. Its facts match the evidence: the cancellerReceiver late-receiver pattern, no AbortController in the sandbox, requestIdleCallback injected (plugins.js:176-181), the user-agent policy, the Springer fixture example (matches fixtures/html/README), and the save path. Splitting the stateless decider (D) from the stateful scheduler (S) is sound. It loses points for a plugin-lifetime PDF MIME handler that breaks its own 'untouched' claim, no memory bound, and a 30 s landing timeout that is still too short for Wiley.
fatal_flaws: A single MIMETypeHandler.addHandlers('application/pdf', ...) is registered for the plugin lifetime and 'returns true only for our browsers, so Zotero's own handling is untouched'. That is false. While any handler exists for the type, the observer replaces the listener on every isDocument PDF channel in the app, buffers the whole PDF, and if no handler returns true falls through to nsIExternalHelperAppService, which shows a download dialog (mimeTypeHandler.js:154-203, 281-324). removeHandlers also deletes the whole type when 1 or fewer handlers remain (:131-134), so a double-removal could remove Zotero's own handler. A and C register by reference count only while captures are in flight.
Landing-page XHR timeout is 30 s with no slow-host profile, against Wiley at 25-37 s and over 60 s twice (08 §3.6). The design cites this evidence but sets a value below the observed range.

No aggregate memory bound: PDFs are whole XHR arraybuffers capped at 200 MB each (streaming via HTTP.download deferred to v1.1). With 4 items x up to 2 hedged OA attempts, the worst case is about 1.6 GB resident. A has a 192 MiB semaphore and C streams to disk.

Item FSM, hedging and parking sequencing live in JS and are verified only against fake ports. The 'JS never inspects URLs or bodies' rule is not enforceable by an ast-grep lint, because JS must read xhr.responseURL, Location/Retry-After headers and browser URLs to build ResponseMeta. The split can drift, as the design admits.

HiddenBrowser.load() 5 s rejection and false return (HiddenBrowser.mjs:183-187, 231-239) is not addressed. The 45 s hidden-browser deadline and 500 ms poll are fine, but anything that awaits load() fails on slow or PDF responses.

Page analysis runs on the main thread, up to about 110 ms per 2 MiB page by the design's own extrapolation. Only requestIdleCallback with a 50 ms timeout mitigates this, and that timeout makes it run anyway. The scheduler also uses wall-clock Date.now() as time, which can jump.
Ledger is counted at complete(), not reserved before the fetch. With 2 institutional requests in flight and the pref written after each PDF, a quit or crash mid-fetch under-counts.

scores.justification: Best fit to the real failure modes in the evidence, and it adopts the fixes the other designs miss. It has a slow-host timeout profile (60 s first byte and 120 s total for Wiley-class hosts, against the 08 §3.6 measurements). The PDF MIME handler is registered only while waiters exist and resolved by topFrameElement per channel. PDFs stream to disk with Zotero.HTTP.download, which exists, uses fetch with credentials:'include' (http.js:636-809) and writes only 2xx bodies (:758-768). Temp storage dirs are ledgered and swept. Untrusted parsing runs in a ChromeWorker with a watchdog (ChromeWorker + wasm verified in 03 §3). There is a single-flight interactive gate, a session FSM (Expired, Ineffective, Refused, Suspended) and parking without a slot. It matches Zotero's ProgressQueue/Dialog API (progressQueue.js, progressQueueDialog.js) and the title/column-label path through Zotero.getString (Fluent for param-less keys: intl.js:131-144). Risks are implementation complexity and a few unverified assumptions, none contradicted by the source.
fatal_flaws: Highest moving-part count: main-thread engine, ChromeWorker analyser, JS executor, and checkpoint+journal replay recovery. Replay depends on strict determinism and on re-emitted effects with fx <= highWater being deduped. It is exercised only by injected traps, so it is the likeliest place for a latent bug. It can be staged (v1: fail the run on a trap) without breaking anything else.

XMP DOI check (S14: 'mismatch rejects') can false-reject valid PDFs. The XMP packet may lie outside the first/last 256 KiB inspected, may be compressed, and AAM/preprint-derived PDFs can carry a different DOI. There is no XMP prevalence data in 05/06. Downgrade to a warning, or require two independent mismatches.

Protocol gaps: the hedge/slow-host rule 'no first byte after 8 s' needs a FirstByte event that is not in the Event list, and BrowserLoad.stop_on (idp_login, challenge_interactive) forces URL classification inside the supposedly dumb executor. Both are fixable but currently inconsistent with the stated boundary.

Unverified: (1) posting a WebAssembly.Module to a ChromeWorker (the fetch-in-worker fallback is sound, 03 §5); (2) a User-Agent header surviving fetch inside HTTP.download. It is probably fine, since VersionHeader leaves a UA without 'Zotero/' untouched (zotero.js:2313-2316) and User-Agent is not a forbidden fetch header, but nobody has run it. For sink:file the design must also pass successCodes:false/errorDelayMax:0, because download() otherwise throws UnexpectedStatusException and _retryOnServerError can loop on 5xx for up to an hour (http.js:1601-1625).

ProgressQueue rows are plain strings rendered without Fluent (progressQueueTable.js renderCell); Zotero.getString with params goes through the .properties bundle, not Fluent (intl.js:131-144). The design's parametrised messages ('Trying { $source }...') therefore have to be pre-formatted with Zotero.ftl.formatValueSync(id, args). Also, the dialog's Close/Cancel buttons call queue.cancel(), which clears all rows of the shared queue (progressQueue.js:140-145).
Licence ledger is counted at complete() and persisted through a debounced 2 s state.json write, not reserved before the fetch. A quit or crash inside that window under-counts institutional PDFs.

Shared with A and B: HiddenBrowser.load() returns false after 5 s or for PDF responses and must not be treated as failure; the doi.org first hop prevents exact per-publisher-host gating of the institutional route.

best_ideas_to_graft: From failure-first (the base): the failure catalogue (F1-F32) as the engine and harness test matrix; the slow-host timeout profile (Wiley-class: 60 s first byte, 120 s total); ChromeWorker analyser with a 3 s watchdog and terminate+respawn; PDF streaming through Zotero.HTTP.download with its own abortReason, byte cap and successCodes:false/errorDelayMax:0; the temp-dir ledger and startup sweep; the single-flight interactive gate with login priority; the session FSM (Expired, Ineffective, Refused, Suspended) with parked items releasing their slot and resuming first; atomic state.json persistence; strict Crossref title matching for items without a DOI; the degradation chain from custom login window to hidden-browser reuse to Open-in-browser to Attach PDF.

From rust-async-engine: the reserve-then-commit licence ledger (persist before the fetch, roll back on a non-PDF); the deterministic sim-test invariants (per-host and global concurrency, spacing, no leaked BodyHandles, no stall) and golden effect traces; the stall watchdog with dump_state; the bytes semaphore for retained bodies; per-channel PDF dispatch keyed on the channel's topFrameElement; fx_stage ownership transfer and the poll-budget 'more' flag. If an async-Rust engine is ever wanted, my probe confirms the Arc<Wake> + thread_local + FuturesUnordered + select_biased! executor builds to a 36 KB zero-import wasm and behaves correctly.

From js-orchestrator-pure-rust: the CancelScope tree plus TaskSet-with-mandatory-catch for the JS executor, since the sandbox has no AbortController (03 §7); a late-safe cancellerReceiver bridge; an idle()/requestIdleCallback gate on main-thread analysis; the cheap synchronous url.classify op for the 500 ms login/browser poll; attach.clean_url and redact.url; meta.build stamp vs manifest version to detect a stale wasm in dev; an async-shaped decider facade so analysis can move to a worker without touching call sites; D/S instance isolation so a parser trap cannot wipe scheduler state.

Mandatory fixes for whichever base is chosen: (1) never treat HiddenBrowser.load() returning false as failure; use an own progress listener and 3 s settle like browserRequest.js:464-483; (2) refcount the PDF MIME handler and guard against double removeHandlers (mimeTypeHandler.js:131-134); (3) slow-host timeouts for Wiley-class hosts; (4) resolve the real publisher host with a no-follow probe, or lease on the redirected host, before applying institutional per-host limits to doi.org and redirector hops; (5) format ProgressQueue messages with Zotero.ftl.formatValueSync(id, args) before updateRow; (6) do not use addDescription for action links.
recommended_base: failure-first. It makes the fewest assumptions that contradict the source, and it is the only design that sets a Wiley-class slow-host timeout profile, registers the PDF handler by reference count, streams PDFs to disk, and sweeps temp dirs. Its engine is a synchronous sans-IO step function, simpler to get right than design A's async Rust executor, which I confirmed is feasible but adds a debugging layer. To keep v1 shippable, stage the risky parts: fail the run on an engine trap instead of checkpoint/journal replay, and defer the XMP hard-reject. Then graft in A's reserve-then-commit ledger and sim invariants, and B's CancelScope/TaskSet JS discipline and idle-gated analysis.
